summary: Defines a connectivity precondition for the Session Description Protocol (SDP) precondition framework. It lets session setup or changes wait until media stream connectivity has been verified, by probing the stream for UDP or by connection establishment for TCP. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: Before starting a game of catch, you check your friend can actually catch. This lets two devices test that data really flows before starting a call.

questions: how to verify media connectivity before sip call

subtitle: A SIP/SDP precondition that holds back a call until the media stream is proven to actually get through.

tldr.problem: A media stream can be negotiated successfully in SDP and still fail, for example because of NATs or firewalls, or because a TCP connection cannot be established.
tldr.mechanism: A new precondition type, conn, delays session establishment or modification until connectivity is verified, using ICE checks, TCP connection establishment or other probing.
tldr.outcome: The called party is not alerted until media connectivity has been confirmed in the requested direction or directions.

today: RFC 5898 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2010. The unit metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on the preconditions framework in RFC 3312 and RFC 4032.

sections.title: Why Check Connectivity First
sections.content:
In SIP, a precondition is a condition that must be satisfied for a media stream before session establishment or modification proceeds. RFC 3312 defines the framework and a Quality of Service precondition. Until preconditions are met, session progress is delayed or the session fails.

A media stream can be agreed in an SDP offer-answer exchange and still not work. With Network Address Translators (NATs) or firewalls in the path, media may never reach the far end, and with TCP the connection-establishment procedures may fail. The connectivity precondition delays session progress until media stream connectivity has been verified. It follows the guidelines for new precondition types in RFC 4032.
sections.eli5: A call can be set up on paper and still not work, like dialing a number where the line is cut. This checks the line first.

sections.title: The conn Precondition Type
sections.content:
The type is the string conn, added to the grammar as precondition-type = "conn" / "sec" / "qos" / token. It is registered with IANA in the Precondition Types used with SIP subregistry.

A mandatory connectivity precondition in an offer delays session establishment or modification until media stream connectivity exists in the desired direction or directions. Alerting of the called party does not happen until then. Only packets needed to verify connectivity SHOULD be sent, so the stream SHOULD NOT be cut through. ICE connectivity checks and TCP SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK packets are examples.

If one media line involves several addresses (for example an RTP stream with RTCP, or a separate FEC stream), connectivity to all of them MUST be verified.
sections.eli5: It is a short code word, conn, that means wait until the line works. The phone will not ring until the check passes, and only test signals go through meanwhile.

sections.title: Status, Direction and Strength
sections.content:
The connectivity precondition MUST be used with the end-to-end status type; use of the segmented type is undefined.

The direction tags mean: send says the sender has sent packets and the other party has received at least one; recv says the other party is sending and this party has received at least one; sendrecv means both hold. A send precondition from the offerer's side is a recv precondition from the answerer's side.

Strength can be mandatory or optional. If an answerer cannot satisfy a mandatory precondition, the offer MUST be rejected. For an optional one, the answerer MUST answer as soon as possible and may raise it to mandatory in the answer. A mandatory precondition needs a SIP Require header with option tag precondition; using an optional precondition with Supported avoids rejection by user agents that lack support.
sections.eli5: You can say send, receive or both ways. And you can say must or nice to have. If the other side cannot do a must, the call is turned down.

sections.title: Verifying Connectivity
sections.content:
The RFC does not require any one verification mechanism. The rules are applied in order. If an explicit mechanism such as ICE is negotiated, the precondition is met when it succeeds. Otherwise, if a connection-oriented transport such as TCP is negotiated, it is met when the connection is established. Otherwise, if the transport or the media data offers an implicit mechanism, that decides. If none applies, connectivity cannot be verified reliably and the precondition will never be satisfied.

With ICE, STUN Binding Requests test candidate address pairs. A full implementation ascertains both send and recv when its own check succeeds for all components. A lite implementation can only act as the controlled agent and learns of send and recv when informed of the nominated pair. It is RECOMMENDED that entities supporting connectivity preconditions also support ICE.

For TCP, a successful three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) satisfies both send and recv, whether requested or not. SCTP SHOULD be treated the same. Because SIP and SDP cannot tie an incoming media packet to a dialog, a UAS MUST NOT require the offerer to confirm a connectivity precondition when no mechanism for that correlation exists.
sections.eli5: The phones can send test pings, like ICE, or just open a connection like TCP. Once a test goes through both ways, they know the line works.

sections.title: Examples and Other Precondition Types
sections.content:
Connectivity alone may not be enough. Quality of Service can be required with the qos precondition from RFC 3312, and security parameter negotiation with the sec precondition from RFC 5027.

The first example uses TCP on a wireless network where nothing, not even a SYN, can be sent before a radio bearer is set up, so both sides offer a=setup:holdconn. Once A is ready it sends an UPDATE with actpass, B chooses active, and when B's bearer is up B opens the TCP connection, then sends 180 Ringing.

The second example uses ICE with a full ICE offerer (A) and a lite ICE answerer (B). A offers a mandatory sendrecv precondition with current status none. B, being lite, asks A to confirm with a=conf:conn e2e send. A runs a successful ICE check and sends an UPDATE with a=curr:conn e2e sendrecv, after which B knows both directions work and proceeds to 180 Ringing.
sections.eli5: In one story the phones wait for their radios, then one opens the line. In the other, one phone tests the line and tells the other, and then the phone rings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General precondition security is covered in RFC 3312 and RFC 4032, which strongly recommend S/MIME integrity protection of the SDP. The RFC adds that an attacker who blocks connectivity checks can stop media sessions from being set up. With preconditions the whole session setup is disrupted, without them only that stream. The RFC provides no defense against an attacker who can block traffic between the endpoints.

An attacker could also forge connectivity checks so endpoints think there is connectivity when there is none, which gives a poor user experience, or try to hijack a connection. The RFC RECOMMENDS that the connectivity-check mechanisms be secured with message authentication and integrity protection, as ICE does.
sections.eli5: Someone could block the test signals so the call never starts, or send fake ones so the phones think the line works. Checking that test signals are genuine helps.
